# Desktop design

Rules for desktop apps, judged on what renders. Apply the shared part and the section of each platform the app ships on; never carry one platform's conventions to another, and keep the native window chrome in every capture.

## Shared core

Judge every rule on the rendered result, from the captures; the rules under Direction before code are the exception, checked as a plan in the worker's report or `DESIGN.md`, not on a render. `(behavior check)` marks a rule no capture can show (a file, a process, an input sequence): Worker.operations runs it and reports it, and nobody infers it from a still. `(preference)` marks taste: list it, do not repair it. A violation of any other rule is judged by this definition:

A discrepancy is material, and starts a repair whatever its size, when it affects acceptance, hierarchy or composition, legibility (cramped, overlapping, clipped or disappearing text), responsiveness at a viewport or size the criteria list, whether text and numbers state the content correctly (a title that misstates what it covers), accessibility, interaction correctness, adherence to a reference or obvious production quality; unnecessary text, headings, cards or badges are design defects. Only pure preference, with none of these effects, stays unrepaired: list it apart, marked optional.

A number is binding only where a platform guideline fixes it; every other number is a default, marked `(default)`, that the design may override with a stated reason.

Apply the skill's capture checklist on the final captures: the worker before reporting, the reviewer in its findings and the root in its own final pass. Critique your own work while you build, with captures wherever the environment can take them. Report only checks actually run, and name each check not run.

### Direction before code

- Name the subject, the audience and the main job, and propose them in the plan when the brief omits them, taking any known preferences or project context as a hint. The brief's own words outrank every avoid list below.
- Draw distinctive choices from the subject itself, its industry, materials and vernacular, and build with the brief's real content throughout: a toy for eight-year-olds and a dashboard for financial analysts should not look related.
- Make deliberate, opinionated choices on palette, type and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk when it is justified.
- Write a compact plan before building: four to six named palette colors with values and roles, type roles, a layout concept in one-sentence prose with ASCII wireframes to compare options and its alignment (left, centered or justified), and two or three principles. Test it with "would I make this for any similar product?" and the competitor test: drop an idea that still works with a competitor's name on it. Revise every part that fails, say what changed and why, and only then write code.
- Say whether this is a refinement, which preserves the existing design, or a redesign, which replaces it.

### Platform fidelity over invention

- Use the platform's own components, navigation and conventions unless the brief gives a reason not to, and brand through the layer the platform leaves open.
- Ported-from-a-website test: a fluent user of the platform never pauses at an off-spec control.
- Rules here are platform concepts. Detect the project's stack and map each rule onto it; never assume one.

### Design record

- Read `DESIGN.md` at the project root before UI work and create or update it after: platform and stack, direction, color roles, type roles, spacing and shape, components and states, do and don't, and a short note of what you tried, so later passes try something new. Note a changed decision instead of silently overwriting it. (behavior check)

### Spend boldness in one place

- One signature detail per screen; everything around it stays quiet and disciplined. Cut decoration that does not serve the brief, remove one accessory before finishing, and replace it with scale, real content or a real image, so the screen is not left thin. (preference)
- A labeled gray placeholder beats drawn art or emoji used as icons. (preference)

### Structure and content

- A structural device (outline, border, divider, eyebrow, label or number) encodes something true about the content and is not decoration. Number items only when the content is a sequence, such as steps or a timeline; check before adding numbers.
- When the brief has no real content, write specific copy and placeholder content from the subject: generic copy makes a design read as templated as generic layout does.

### Copy

- Words are design content, not decoration. Before writing, ask what the screen has to say and the simplest way to say it; each written element does one job.
- Write from the user's side, naming things as users understand them (notifications, not webhook config). Say what something is or does and do not sell it; specific and legible beats clever.
- Use active voice, plain verbs, sentence case (or the platform's own capitalization) and no filler, with a tone that fits the brand and the audience.
- A control says exactly what happens ("Save changes", not "Submit"), and an action keeps one name through the whole flow: the Archive button leads to an "Archived" confirmation.
- Failure and emptiness give direction. An error says what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice and without apology or vagueness; an empty screen invites the next action.

### Quality floor, unannounced

- Text contrast is at least 4.5:1 and non-text control contrast at least 3:1. Color is never the only signal, and the palette is harmonious.
- Every state exists and is captured where reachable: hover or press, focus, disabled, loading, empty, error and long content.
- The system's reduced-motion, larger-text and high-contrast settings, where the platform has them, change the render.

## Shared desktop rules

- Design to the window, not the screen, and reflow smoothly at every width. Symptom: clipped or stranded content when the window narrows.
- Everything the pointer can do, the keyboard can do. Tab order follows visual order, arrows move inside composite controls, and a custom focusable element shows a visible focus indicator. (behavior check)
- Shortcuts are discoverable in menus and tooltips.
- The app follows the system light or dark theme, accent color, text scale and high-contrast mode. A hard-coded color that breaks high contrast is a defect.
- Desktop is denser than mobile, but frequent or high-consequence targets get more room.
- Settings are few, have good defaults, apply immediately and do not duplicate system options.

## Windows

- Standard controls align to 40×40 epx and compact ones to 32×32 epx, on a 4 epx grid, with 8 epx between buttons.
- The title bar is 32 px high. Empty space drags the window, right-click shows the system menu, and double-click toggles maximize. (behavior check)
- Caption buttons sit at the right and stay fully visible, so the title truncates first. The bar dims when the window is inactive. Capture both.
- Direct manipulation comes first, then a command bar, and a menu bar for complex apps. Context menus hold secondary commands.
- Accelerators are Ctrl plus a letter and access keys are Alt plus a letter; F6 and Shift+F6 cycle the panes. (behavior check)
- Use the system font and its ramp, sentence case, semibold instead of bold, and no italics. The accent marks emphasis and state, sparingly.
- Mica is for windows and acrylic only for transient surfaces. Contrast themes are not dark mode and are captured on their own.

## macOS

- System window frames and controls, never custom chrome. Default control size is 28×28 pt with 20×20 pt as the minimum.
- Text is 13 pt by default with 10 pt as the minimum. There is no dynamic text size, so use the system font roles.
- The menu bar keeps the standard order: App, File, Edit, Format, View, the app's own menus, Window, Help. Unavailable items are dimmed, not hidden.
- Settings lives in the app menu and opens with Cmd+comma; the toolbar has no settings button. Standard shortcuts keep their meaning, and one is reused only when its standard action does not exist in the app. Full Keyboard Access works. (behavior check)
- Toolbars are customizable and monochrome over colorful content, with short titles that are never the app name.
- Sheets are modal; a long task gets a window. Glass belongs to the control layer, and content uses standard materials with vibrancy.

## GNOME

- The header bar puts main actions at the start, the title or view switcher in the center and menus at the end. Controls are few, flat icon buttons with tooltips, and drag space always remains.
- The primary menu sits at the end of the header bar and holds Preferences, Keyboard Shortcuts, Help and About, with no Quit or Close item.
- Shortcuts use Ctrl, and Shift+Ctrl reverses; never Alt (access keys) or Super (system). F10 opens the menu and Esc closes transient views. (behavior check)
- Design from the narrowest size up. Support at least 1024×600, and down to 360×294 for phone-capable apps. Content width is capped in large windows.
- Use the system font and text styles, with no italics, no all caps and no text over images.
- Default to light and follow the system preference; offer light, dark and system when an in-app choice exists, and never hard-code an accent the system provides.
- Settings use boxed lists with one control per row, two at most.

## Refuse list

Unless the brief asks for it:

- custom window chrome or caption buttons
- one platform's menu bar, shortcuts or settings placement on another
- a hamburger menu that holds the primary commands of a desktop app
- hard-coded colors that ignore the system theme and high contrast
- a mobile layout stretched across a wide window

## Capture checklist

Capture narrow, default and wide window widths, each in light, dark and high contrast, and, where the platform has a text scale, at 150% or 200%. Add a keyboard-only focus traversal, the open menus, an inactive window and a dialog or sheet. Show the native window chrome in every capture.
